lead: A linear first-order equation has the shape y′ + P(x)y = Q(x). The unknown y and its derivative appear only to the first power. Such equations model circuits, cooling, mixing and money growth. One multiplication by a cleverly chosen function turns the left side into the derivative of a product. After that, a single integration gives the solution. The function is called the integrating factor, and some syllabi call the method Leibnitz's linear equation.
prereq: You need: the integration practice of 1.2 and the integrating-factor idea of 1.4.

sections.h3: Standard form and the integrating factor

blocks.text: A first-order linear equation is y′ + P(x)y = Q(x). Here y′ = dy/dx, P(x) and Q(x) are continuous functions on an interval I, and y is the unknown function. The coefficient of y′ must be 1. If an equation arrives as a(x)y′ + b(x)y = c(x), divide by a(x) first; this step is where many marks are lost.

The left side y′ + P y does not integrate directly. Multiply the whole equation by a positive function μ(x), still unknown. The left becomes μ y′ + μ P y. The product rule gives (μ y)′ = μ y′ + μ′ y. These match exactly when μ′ = μ P. Solving dμ/dx = P μ separates to dμ/μ = P dx, so ln μ = ∫P dx and μ = e<sup>∫P dx</sup>.

blocks.where: μ is the integrating factor; P is the coefficient of y in standard form; use any one antiderivative of P, with no added constant.

blocks.text: This μ is the integrating factor, shortened IF. Adding a constant to ∫P dx only multiplies μ by a constant, which cancels later, so choose the simplest antiderivative. The IF is always positive. Some syllabi call this Leibnitz's linear equation; others call it the first-order linear equation. Section 1.4 reaches the same idea from exactness; here it is a direct product-rule trick.
After multiplying by μ, the equation becomes (μ y)′ = μ Q. Integrate both sides with respect to x: μ y = ∫ μ Q dx + C, where C is the constant of integration. Divide by μ.
y = μ<sup>−1</sup>(∫ Q μ dx + C)
blocks.where: y is the solution; μ = e<sup>∫P dx</sup>; C is fixed by an initial condition; all integrals are with respect to x.

items: Write the equation in standard form, with coefficient 1 on y′.
Read P and Q; keep the sign of P.
Compute μ = e<sup>∫P dx</sup> using one antiderivative.
Multiply both sides by μ and replace the left side by (μ y)′.
Integrate once: μ y = ∫ μ Q dx + C.
Divide by μ, then use y(x₀)=y₀ to find C.

blocks.text: A short check: y′ + 2y = e<sup>−x</sup> has P=2, Q=e<sup>−x</sup>, μ=e<sup>2x</sup>. Then (y e<sup>2x</sup>)′ = e<sup>x</sup>, so y e<sup>2x</sup> = e<sup>x</sup> + C and y = e<sup>−x</sup> + C e<sup>−2x</sup>.

In a series RL circuit, L di/dt + R i = E(t). L is inductance in henry, R is resistance in ohm, E(t) is applied voltage in volt, i is current in ampere, and t is time in second. Divide by L: i′ + (R/L)i = E(t)/L. The IF is e<sup>Rt/L</sup>. If E is a constant E₀, i = E₀/R + C e<sup>−Rt/L</sup>; the first term is the steady current and the second decays with time constant L/R.

Some equations become linear after a substitution. Suppose the equation can be written f′(y) dy/dx + P(x) f(y) = Q(x). Here f is a known differentiable function. Put u = f(y). Then du/dx = f′(y) dy/dx by the chain rule. The equation becomes u′ + P(x)u = Q(x), which is linear in u. Solve it by the integrating factor, then invert y = f<sup>−1</sup>(u).

items: Bernoulli case: for y′ + P y = Q yn, take f(y)=y1−n. The equation is linear in u=y1−n; the full method is in 1.6.
Root case: for y′/(2√y) + P√y = Q with y>0, take u=√y. Then u′ = y′/(2√y), so u′ + P u = Q, linear in u. The equation y′ + P√y = Q itself does not have this form and is not linearized this way.
Log case: for y′/y + P ln y = Q with y>0, take u=ln y. Then u′ = y′/y, so u′ + P u = Q, linear in u. The equation y′ + P ln y = Q is not of this template form.

blocks.text: After solving for u, invert only on the interval where f has an inverse. Check the original equation, because the substitution can lose solutions where f′(y)=0 or where a division by y<sup>n</sup> was made.

figure.caption: The pipeline from standard form to the integrating factor, the product derivative, and the final one-line integration. Notice that the factor is built from P alone; Q enters only on the right.

spec.title: The integrating factor
spec.aria: A top-to-bottom pipeline builds the integrating factor, multiplies, writes the left side as one derivative, and integrates.

examples.question: Solve the initial value problem x dy/dx + 2y = x², y(1)=1. State the interval and find y(2).
steps: For x>0, divide by x: dy/dx + (2/x)y = x. Standard form has P=2/x and Q=x.
IF μ = e<sup>∫(2/x)dx</sup> = e<sup>2 ln x</sup> = x². No constant is needed; x>0 keeps ln x real.
The left side is (x² y)′ because d(x² y)/dx = x² y′ + 2x y. Hence (x² y)′ = x³.
examples.answer: The solution is y = x²/4 + 3/(4x²) on x>0, with C=3/4, and y(2)=1.1875; x and y are treated as dimensionless here.
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction
C = Fraction(3, 4)
x = Fraction(2, 1)
y = x**2 / 4 + C / x**2
print(float(C))
print(float(y))

traps: Standard form first: in x y′+2y=x², P is 2/x after division, not 2.
The sign of P stays inside the integral: y′−3y=1 gives μ=e<sup>−3x</sup>, not e<sup>3x</sup>.
Use one antiderivative for ∫P dx; a constant only rescales μ and cancels.
Q must be the right side after division by the coefficient of y′, and any x=0 division removes the point x=0 from the interval.
The left side becomes (μ y)′, not μ′ y′; check the product before integrating.

quiz.q: State the standard form of a first-order linear equation and the formula for its integrating factor.
quiz.a: Standard form: y′ + P(x)y = Q(x); integrating factor μ = e<sup>∫P dx</sup>.

quiz.q: Why does multiplying by μ turn the left side into one derivative?
quiz.a: Because (μ y)′ = μ y′ + μ′ y, and μ′ = Pμ makes μ′ y equal μ P y, exactly the extra term.
P=3, Q=6, μ=e<sup>3x</sup>. Then (y e<sup>3x</sup>)′=6e<sup>3x</sup>, so y e<sup>3x</sup>=2e<sup>3x</sup>+C and y=2+C e<sup>−3x</sup>. y(0)=2 gives C=0, so y=2.

quiz.q: Solve x y′ + y = x² for x>0 with y(1)=0.
quiz.a: Divide: y′+(1/x)y=x, so μ=x. Then (xy)′=x², xy=x³/3+C, y=x²/3+C/x. y(1)=0 gives C=−1/3, so y=x²/3−1/(3x).

quiz.q: A student reads P=2 from x y′ + 2y = x². What is wrong, and what is the correct IF?
quiz.a: The equation is not in standard form because the coefficient of y′ is x. Divide by x to get P=2/x and Q=x, so μ=e<sup>∫(2/x)dx</sup>=x², not e<sup>2x</sup>.

quiz.q: For y′ − 3y = 1, why is the integrating factor e<sup>−3x</sup> rather than e<sup>3x</sup>?
quiz.a: Here P=−3. The formula μ=e<sup>∫P dx</sup> gives e<sup>−3x</sup>; the sign of P stays inside the integral.

quiz.q: Can y′ = y² be solved directly as a linear equation? Explain.
quiz.a: No, y² makes it nonlinear in y. It is a Bernoulli equation with n=2; the substitution u=y−1 gives a linear equation, as in 1.6.

beyond: Not for the exam. Linear first-order equations are the continuous-time building block of control engineering, pharmacokinetics and RC/RL circuit analysis. In research, the same integrating factor appears in linear ODE systems and in the method of variation of constants. Numerical packages such as SciPy solve these equations with adaptive step sizes when P and Q are messy. Search for integrating factor linear ODE, RL circuit time constant, and variation of parameters for the next step.
